chunks: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) forbade a man from performing 'tadbeeh' in prayer as a donkey performs 'tadbeeh'.
Its meaning is that a man lowers his head during the bowing (ruku') until it is lower than his back.
When he (peace be upon him and his family) used to bow, he did not make his head upright nor did he raise it excessively.
Its meaning is that he did not raise it so that it would be higher than his body, but it was in between.
'Al-Iqna'' (raising/leveling) is raising the head and making it distinct/upright.
Allah, Exalted is He, said: «Racing ahead, their heads raised up» [14:43].
What is recommended from this is that a man's back and head are leveled during the bowing.
Because the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), when he bowed, if water was poured on his back, it would remain firm/settled.
Al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) said: «There is no prayer for the one who does not make firm his spine during his bowing and prostration.»

key_terms.اسْتَقَرَّ: To remain firm, settled, or stable.
key_terms.الرُّكُوع: Bowing, a fundamental pillar of the Islamic prayer.
key_terms.الْإِقْنَاع: Raising the head to a level position; distinct from full upright or full low.
key_terms.صَلْبُهُ: His spine or back; referring to the rigidity and straightness of the back during bowing.
key_terms.يَدْبَحُ: To slaughter or cut; here used metaphorically for the specific motion of bowing.

ai.seo_question: What is the correct head and back posture for ruku' in Shia prayer?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Mani al-Akhbar* clarifies the precise geometric alignment of the Prophet’s (SAW) ruku’, distinguishing between 'iqna'' (raising the head) and excessive lowering, using the vivid imagery of water settling on his back to denote stability. It links this physical discipline to the spiritual validity of prayer, as emphasized by Imam al-Sadiq (AS), who insisted that a firm spine is a prerequisite for a valid prayer, reflecting the Shia emphasis on both outward form and inner presence. The prohibition against bowing like a donkey underscores the need for dignified, controlled humility rather than mere mechanical submission.
